findings.headline: Strategic housing alternatives to bed and breakfast accommodation delivering £0.463m underspend through direct matches and private sector leasing scheme
findings.detail: An underspend of £0.463m is forecast on temporary bed and breakfast accommodation for homeless households. The council attributes this to initiatives offering direct matches to social housing and a private sector leasing scheme as alternatives to B&B. The paper describes this as a "continued result" of these initiatives, suggesting a sustained programme.
findings.matters: Demonstrates that demand-side interventions creating alternatives to expensive temporary accommodation can reduce costs while maintaining service availability.
findings.figures: B&B underspend £0.463m
findings.quote: An underspend of (£0.463m) is forecast at Qtr. 1. relating to temporary B&B accommodation. This is as a continued result of initiatives offering alternatives to B&B accommodation through direct matches and the private sector leasing scheme.

findings.headline: Insurance costs reduced by £0.410m following contract renegotiation, delivering unexpected saving not forecast at budget setting
findings.detail: An underspend of £0.410m is forecast on insurance costs following successful renegotiation of the council's insurance contract. The council had budgeted for continued cost inflation based on historical trends, but the new contract delivered materially lower costs than previously anticipated.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the value of active commercial management; budget setting based on historical trends can miss genuine cost reduction opportunities.
findings.figures: Insurance underspend £0.410m
findings.quote: The main reason for the underspend against insurance is in relation to the reduction in the insurance premium costs for this financial year. A new contract/tender was negotiated which resulted in a significant reduction in costs.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £58.9m to £933.704m; council pursuing short-term borrowing strategy at 4-4.5% due to elevated PWLB rates of 5-6.5%
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement has increased from £874.810m at 31 March 2026 to £933.704m at 30 June 2026, an increase of £58.9m. Total external debt (including PFI and finance leases) stands at £661.016m. The council remains in a need-to-borrow position and is deploying a short-term borrowing strategy at 4-4.5% to avoid longer-term rates of 5-6.5%.
findings.matters: The rising CFR and short-term borrowing strategy expose the council to refinancing risk if rates do not fall, and create dependence on functioning debt markets.
findings.figures: CFR increased from £874.810m to £933.704m (+£58.9m); total external debt £661.016m; short-term rates 4.0-4.5%; PWLB 5-year rates 5.04-5.49%; PWLB 20-year rates 6.02-6.50%
findings.quote: Short to medium term borrowing is still a favourable position with interest rates remaining elevated, the strategy is to borrow in the short to medium term to alleviate any cash flow requirements – whist monitoring and taking advantage of longer term borrowing when rates are favourable.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve balance of £15.818m represents 3.99% of revenue budget, positioned at the lower end of the council's 3-5% policy range
findings.detail: At 30 June 2026, the General Fund balance stands at £15.818m, which represents 3.99% of the £407.569m net revenue budget. This falls within the council's stated reserves policy of 3-5%, but is positioned at the lower end of that range. The Budget Risk reserve, which provides additional buffer for in-year pressures, is £6.975m but forecast to move to £5.571m after committed transfers.
findings.matters: Reserves at the lower end of policy indicate limited headroom for unexpected pressures or forecast underperformance.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £15.818m (3.99% of budget); policy range 3-5%; Budget Risk Reserve £6.975m moving to £5.571m
findings.quote: At 30 June 2026, the General Fund Balance is £15.818m, which represents around 3.99% of the revenue budget. This is in line with the council's reserves policy for the General Fund Balance of between 3 and 5% of the net revenue budget.

findings.headline: Capital programme shows £30.293m variance against original budget including major scheme slippages: Derby Theatre Levelling Up Fund £5.822m, Guildhall LUF £0.904m, HRA Rivermead £2.878m
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme forecast is £227.272m against the original approved budget of £196.979m. Major slippages include: Derby Theatre Levelling Up Fund slipped £5.822m due to protracted landlord negotiations; Guildhall LUF slipped £0.904m (project still in design with planning application pending); HRA Rivermead refurbishment slipped £2.878m due to delayed options review; and Abbey Lodge slipped £3.201m due to additional works required.
findings.matters: Major capital programme slippages affect borrowing requirement profiles and extend the period over which capital must be financed, potentially increasing financing costs.
findings.figures: Total variance £30.293m; Derby Theatre £5.822m; Guildhall £0.904m; Rivermead £2.878m; Abbey Lodge £3.201m; forecast spend £227.272m vs original budget £196.979m
findings.quote: Slippage of (£5.822m) required due to delays caused by protracted negotiations between the grant recipient and their landlord, to gain an agreement for the proposed construction works.

findings.headline: Adult social care forecast pressure of £0.889m driven by 13% demand growth in community support, 8% residential placement cost inflation, and 33 new transitions from children's services
findings.detail: Adult social care is forecasting an £0.889m pressure from multiple drivers: 33 children transitioning to adult services at estimated cost of £1.137m; residential placement costs rising 8% year-on-year to an average of £1,979 per week; and demand for community-based support up 13% in the past year. The council notes that pressures are concentrated in younger adults requiring specialist care.
findings.matters: The 13% demand growth in community support and 8% cost inflation on residential placements suggest ongoing structural cost pressure beyond planned transitions from children's services.
findings.figures: £0.889m forecast pressure; 33 transitions at £1.137m; residential costs up 8% to £1,979/week; community demand up 13%
findings.quote: The pressures for client care costs are mostly being identified within the younger adult's cohort who require specialist care. In the last 12 months the number of clients receiving care in residential settings has remained stable however the cost of a residential placement has seen an increase of 8% and is currently an average weekly cost of £1,979. While the cost of younger adults being supported in the community has remained stable the demand has increased by 13% since this time last year.

findings.headline: Children's residential care placements increased 40% to 46 from 33 one year ago, driving £1.368m budget pressure at average cost of £0.420m per placement
findings.detail: The council has experienced an unexpected increase in external agency residential placements for children in care, from 33 to 46 placements. Simultaneously, independent fostering placements fell from 224 to 197. The average cost of residential care is £0.420m per child per year compared to £0.061m for fostering. This mix shift towards more expensive placements is driving a £1.368m forecast pressure against a £53m total placement budget.
findings.matters: The 40% increase in expensive residential placements (£0.420m vs £0.061m for fostering) is creating material cost pressure despite overall children in care numbers falling.
findings.figures: Residential placements increased from 33 to 46 (40% increase); fostering placements fell from 224 to 197; average residential cost £0.420m; average fostering cost £0.061m; budget pressure £1.368m
findings.quote: The pressure is due to the unexpected increase in cost and number of placements in external (agency) residential homes. Whilst the total number of children in care has reduced from 546 in May 2025 to 514 in May 2026, Derby has seen an increase in the demand for agency residential, from 33 placements at May 2025 to 46 placements at May 2026...The average cost of placements in residential care is £0.420m per year compared to the average cost of an Independent Fostering Agency at £0.061m.

findings.headline: 87% of savings target delivered; £0.915m Council Wide Delivery Board aspirational saving unachieved with no firm mitigation proposals identified
findings.detail: The council forecast delivery of £6.190m of its £7.105m savings target (87%), with the only shortfall being the £0.915m Council Wide aspirational savings target. The monitoring report states explicitly that "to date, no new savings have been delivered" against this target, and notes that alternatives are being investigated but "no firm proposals as yet to mitigate."
findings.matters: Unachieved savings targets represent unmitigated budget risk; with 0% Q1 delivery and no mitigation plan identified, the £0.915m gap may materialise as revenue pressure unless addressed.
findings.figures: £7.105m total target; £6.190m forecast delivery; £0.915m unachieved (0% delivery rate)
findings.quote: There is a Council Wide aspirational target of £0.915m savings for Delivery Boards to continue to drive for efficiencies and savings. To date, no new savings have been delivered.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit of £33.247m eligible for 90% government grant, but conditional on approval of council's SEND Reform Plan
findings.detail: The 2026/27 in-year DSG deficit is forecast at £9.973m, bringing the cumulative deficit to £33.247m. All councils with DSG deficits can access a High Needs Stability Grant covering up to 90% of their accumulated deficit up to end 2025/26, but the grant is only paid once the council's SEND Reform Plan has been approved. The paper confirms local authorities will not receive payments until this approval is secured.
findings.matters: A £33m DSG deficit is material; the 90% grant would cover most but is contingent on SEND Reform Plan approval, so the approval status is critical to understanding the council's true revenue position.
findings.figures: £9.973m in-year deficit; £33.247m cumulative deficit; eligible for up to 90% government grant
findings.quote: All local authorities with a DSG deficit will be eligible in 2026/27 to receive a High Needs Stability Grant covering up to 90% of their DSG deficit accrued up to the end of 2025/26. This grant will only be paid once each local authority has secured approval of their local area's Local SEND Reform Plan.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme supported by PWLB borrowing at 0.4% discount (available until March 2027); 311 affordable homes planned
findings.detail: Council used PWLB HRA rate (0.4% below standard certainty rate) to support housing revenue account capital investment in 2025/26 and plans continued borrowing in 2026/27 while discounted rate remains available. HRA capital programme includes delivery of 311 new affordable homes over 2025/26 to 2028/29 forecast period. HRA CFR growing from £208.6m (2025/26) to £254.7m (2028/29).
findings.matters: Shows active investment in affordable housing delivery supported by subsidized borrowing rate; demonstrates strategic housing priorities and use of time-limited funding support.
findings.figures: 311 new affordable homes planned over forecast period; HRA CFR £208.6m (2025/26) forecast to £254.7m (2028/29); PWLB HRA discount 0.4% available until March 2027
findings.quote: The HRA capital programme was supported by borrowing in 2025/26 and further borrowing is planned over the medium term. The Council will be utilising the discounted rate in 2026/27 to support the HRA.

findings.headline: Two breaches of banking minimum balance requirement in 2025/26; both low-risk, approved by S151, and incurred no penalties
findings.detail: Q1 2025: minimum balance with banking provider breached (previously reported to Cabinet). Q3 2025: breach occurred and was approved by Section 151 Officer due to need for large cash balance to guarantee property purchase completion early next day. Both breaches were low-risk and incurred no penalties. All other treasury management compliance requirements met during the year.
findings.matters: Governance framework for treasury management requires monitoring; low-risk breaches with proper approval show controls are functioning and exceptions are properly managed.
findings.figures: Two breaches of minimum balance requirements; no penalties or financial impact
findings.quote: All treasury management activities undertaken up to 31 March 2026 complied with the principles of the Treasury Management Code and the Council's internal Treasury Management Strategy, with the exception of two breaches relating to the minimum balance required to be held with the Council's banking provider.

findings.headline: Forecast total external borrowing to increase from £581.6m to £825.1m by 2029/30; financing costs rising to 8% of revenue stream
findings.detail: Medium-term forecasts show rising borrowing requirement as capital programme accelerates and internal resources decline. Total external borrowing forecast to increase from £581.6m (actual 2025/26) to £825.1m (2029/30). Capital financing requirement (CFR) increasing from £874.7m (2025/26) to £995.9m (2028/29) due to capital programme and IFRS16 lease recognition. Associated financing costs (interest and MRP) forecast to rise from £23.2m (2025/26) to £35.9m (2027/28), increasing as proportion of net revenue stream from 7% to 8%.
findings.matters: Material increase in future borrowing requirement indicates sustained capital investment programme and rising debt burden; critical to lender assessment of future financial position and affordability.
findings.figures: External borrowing forecast £581.6m (2025/26) to £825.1m (2029/30); interim forecasts £681.1m (2027/28), £779m (2028/29); CFR forecast £874.7m to £995.9m; financing costs rising from £23.2m (7% of revenue) to £35.9m (8% of revenue)
findings.quote: The CFR has increased between 2024/25 and 2025/26 due to the Councils capital programme and the implementation of IFRS16 bringing the recognition of assets and liabilities onto the balance sheet for leases.

findings.headline: Capital programme experienced delays in delivery, with expenditure slipping into following year
findings.detail: A number of schemes within the approved capital programme did not spend as forecast, resulting in expenditure slipping into 2026/27. This created the timing gap that resulted in higher cash balances during 2025/26 and the investment opportunities that generated excess investment income. Forward capital programme forecasts show continued significant expenditure over 2026-29.
findings.matters: Indicates delivery risk or timing risk in capital plan execution; affects cash forecasting and future year spending commitments and borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure slipped to future years; capital programme forecast 2026/27 £225.2m, 2027/28 £160m, 2028/29 £86m
findings.quote: A number of schemes within the approved capital programme experienced delays in delivery, resulting in expenditure being slipped into the following year.

findings.headline: Actual borrowing of £581.6m came in £115.966m below budget of £697.5m
findings.detail: Strong cash position and capital programme delays meant the council did not need to borrow as much as budgeted. Net borrowing requirement improved to £471.9m from prior year position of £511.4m, reflecting good cash management and benefit of higher temporary investment balances. Council remained in underlying need to borrow but funded more from existing resources and temporary cash than anticipated.
findings.matters: Signals better near-term financial position and lower interest costs than planned, though partly driven by temporary factors and capital slippage.
findings.figures: Actual borrowing £581.558m vs budget £697.524m (underspend £115.966m); net borrowing £471.876m vs prior year £511.409m; total investments £109.682m vs prior year £66.115m
findings.quote: Actual total debt is £581.6m and total investments are £109.7m compared to £577.5m and £66.1m as at 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: Investment income of £4.652m generated on average cash balance of £114.4m, significantly above budget, from capital programme timing delays
findings.detail: Higher cash balances resulted from timing differences between taking out long-term borrowing and delays in planned capital expenditure. Rather than deploy surplus immediately, the council invested it in accordance with treasury strategy. Interest earned totalled £4.652m (2024/25: £2.898m) despite lower return rate of 3.81%, on average portfolio of £114.431m (budget £30m). Council states this investment income supported financial resilience during volatile interest rate period.
findings.matters: Demonstrates active management of temporary cash surpluses and strong yield on cash position, though gains are partly temporary due to capital delays.
findings.figures: Interest earned £4.652m (2025/26) vs £2.898m (2024/25); average portfolio £114.431m vs budget £30m; return rate 3.81%
findings.quote: The average size of the deposit/investment portfolio held higher balances through to Q4, this is as a result of the timing between taking out Long Term borrowing and delays in planned expenditure (capital spend).

findings.headline: Council restructured two long-term loans, reducing term and securing lower interest rates, with a cash benefit achieved
findings.detail: Arlingclose identified an opportunity to restructure two long-term loans. The restructuring reduced the loan term, secured lower interest rates, and changed the repayment profile so principal is repaid over three years. The council achieved a cash benefit that has been included in year-end accounts.
findings.matters: Shows active debt portfolio management and cost reduction, lowering future interest payments and improving treasury position.
findings.figures: Two loans restructured; cash benefit amount not separately quantified
findings.quote: This involved reducing the loan term, securing lower interest rates, and changing the repayment profile so that the principal is repaid over three years. As a result of these changes, the Council achieved a cash benefit, which has been included in the year-end accounts.

findings.headline: Property portfolio and maintenance backlog risk improved following Q3 review
findings.detail: Strategic risk SR44, concerning aging and inappropriate property and maintenance backlog, was reviewed in Q3 as its score had remained static for several quarters. An in-depth review with the Improvement Officer and risk updater resulted in the risk score being reduced, indicating progress on managing this known capital liability.
findings.matters: Deferred property maintenance represents a material contingent liability; lenders and peer councils track whether councils are actively managing known capital constraints or letting them accumulate.
findings.figures: No specific quantification of property portfolio size, backlog value or risk score movement provided.
findings.quote: This risk was identified for review during Q3 as the mitigated risk position had remained unchanged for several quarters. The Improvement Officer met with the risk updater and worked through the challenge template together. Risk position at Q3 was reduced.

findings.headline: Strategic risks remain above the council's own tolerance and target scores
findings.detail: The paper reports that current mitigated risk scores for strategic risks are, on the whole, higher than either the council's tolerance or target scores. The council characterises this as reflecting ambitious target-setting and active management efforts to achieve lower risk positions, rather than indicating failure to manage risk.
findings.matters: A peer council or lender assessing the council's risk maturity needs to know both that risks are elevated and that the council is actively managing toward targets; this transparency signals realistic target-setting and ongoing control efforts.
findings.figures: No specific quantification of risk scores provided.
findings.quote: It should be noted that on the whole the current mitigated risk scores for strategic risks are higher than either the tolerance or target score – this reflects the ambition to get to a low mitigated risk position rather than a failure to manage risk.

findings.headline: MTFP sustainability risk score reduced, primarily due to fairer funding settlement rather than internal mitigation
findings.detail: Strategic risk SR15, concerning the council's ability to deliver a balanced medium-term financial plan and protect future financial sustainability, was reviewed during Q3 assurance activities. The risk score was reduced, but explicitly because of the fairer funding settlement, not from risk control or mitigation actions taken by the council. This indicates that improvement in the council's financial position reflects external funding factors rather than structural solutions.
findings.matters: A lender or peer finance director needs to distinguish whether financial improvement is durable or depends on external funding conditions; this case was primarily the latter, affecting assessments of medium-term sustainability.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided; risk score reduction noted but not quantified.
findings.quote: Note that the risk position has been reduced following that, but more as a result of the fairer funding settlement than the risk review itself.

findings.headline: External Audit made recommendation that council maintain effective governance arrangements for Local Government Reorganisation transition.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 Value for Money Report (February 2026) made two recommendations, one of which called on the council to maintain effective and transparent governance arrangements for LGR, with the Audit and Governance Committee to seek specific assurance on key controls supporting the transition once plans are finalised.
findings.matters: External Audit's explicit flagging of LGR governance as a risk area signals that the audit firm expects heightened scrutiny of transition controls; this is material to other councils planning similar restructures.
findings.figures: Recommendation issued in 2024/25 Value for Money Report, February 2026
findings.quote: The Council needs to maintain effective and transparent governance arrangements in the progression of plans for local government reorganisation (LGR), including effective leadership and the audit and governance committee should seek specific assurance once plans are finalised, over the key controls in place to support the transition to a new organisation.

findings.headline: Internal Audit work in SEND service has not commenced due to capacity constraints driven by inspection readiness.
findings.detail: Audit activity in SEND has been deferred to allow service capacity to focus on inspection preparation, creating a governance gap. The action plan indicates audit will commence post-inspection (anticipated autumn/winter 2026) once service capacity is released.
findings.matters: Deferred audit in a high-risk service area (SEND is subject to combined Ofsted/CQC inspection in 2026/27) creates assurance gap and raises questions about whether operational pressure is preventing governance oversight.
findings.figures: SEND audit not commenced; anticipated restart autumn/winter 2026 post-inspection
findings.quote: Audit activity has not commenced within SEND due to capacity issues in light of inspection readiness.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation proposals submitted, with Government decision expected July 2026 and new unitary authorities to launch April 2028.
findings.detail: Derby and nine other Derbyshire councils submitted LGR proposals in November 2025 proposing a north/south two-unitary model. Pre-decision phase work has focused on Day 1 requirements and assurance. Shadow authorities are expected April 2027 with elections May 2027, and the new unitary councils to launch April 2028. This creates governance and planning uncertainty for a 24-month period before merger.
findings.matters: Structural change of this scale creates planning uncertainty for lenders and peer councils assessing financial sustainability beyond the merger date; it also affects leadership stability and officer retention.
findings.figures: Government decision expected July 2026; shadow authorities April 2027; elections May 2027; new authorities April 2028; proposal submitted November 2025
findings.quote: A Government decision is expected in July 2026. Subject to this, the new shadow authorities are expected to be in place by April 2027, with elections to be held in May 2027. The new unitary authorities are expected to be launched in April 2028.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing undertaken to manage cash flow due to historic low reserves, all within prudential indicators.
findings.detail: The council was forced into temporary borrowing to smooth cash flows when reserves were at historic lows. Borrowing activity remained within the Treasury Management Strategy's prudential indicators. This is a symptom of the reserve depletion mentioned in the financial resilience section, now resolved through the rebuild to 4.6%.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing to cover daily cash flow is a sign of underlying structural pressure and carries operational risk; lenders and peers note whether this trend is reversing (it is here, via reserve rebuild).
findings.figures: Historic low reserves requiring short-term borrowing; all within prudential indicators
findings.quote: Due to the historic low levels of reserves the Council has had to undertake some short-term borrowing to manage cash flows, with all activity within the permitted prudential indicators set out in the Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block in cumulative deficit of £23.274m with in-year deficit of £7m; government providing up to 90% grant mitigation.
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs Block is in structural deficit (a national picture affecting all councils), but the government has responded by providing a DSG deficit grant of up to 90% of the accumulated balance. This is described as 'an excellent response' in the document. A deficit management plan is in place. SEND reforms are proposed and intended to create a sustainable position going forward.
findings.matters: DSG deficits can cascade into general fund pressure if not managed; this council has a material shortfall but government support materially reduces the council's own cost of resolution. Peer councils use this to benchmark their own DSG position.
findings.figures: High Needs Block cumulative deficit £23.274m; in-year deficit £7m; government grant up to 90% of accumulated balance
findings.quote: The High Needs Block of the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) is in a cumulative deficit position of £23.274m with an in-year deficit of £7m. This is a national picture, and the Government have responded by providing a DSG deficit grant of up to 90% of the accumulated balance. This is an excellent response

findings.headline: Five consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions on Statement of Accounts (2020/21 to 2024/25), likely to continue for 2025/26.
findings.detail: Ernst & Young disclaimed opinions for 2020/21–2023/24 due to resourcing issues and a national pause on assurance over infrastructure and pension assets. Replacement auditor Forvis Mazars issued a further disclaimed opinion for 2024/25 due to lack of assurance on prior year balances and is expected to do so again for 2025/26. The council's own timetabled account publication is not the constraint; the audit backlog is.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions prevent stakeholders—lenders, regulators, and council members—from relying on the financial position. A five-year backlog flags material uncertainty about the council's true financial state and is unusual even by post-pandemic audit standards.
findings.figures: 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 disclaimed; 2024/25 disclaimed; 2025/26 likely to be disclaimed
findings.quote: the Accounts for 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 receiving a disclaimed audit opinion... Our current auditors, Forvis Mazars, issued a further disclaimed opinion for 2024/25 and will likely do so for 2025/26 due to the lack of assurance of prior year balances.

findings.headline: Draft outturn for 2025/26 shows £4.066m underspend with 100% delivery of planned savings.
findings.detail: The council has delivered an underspend, meaning no further reserve drawdown and a further replenishment. Children's Services underspent for the first time in several years, attributed to successful prevention and early help services. The full delivery of savings targets indicates improved control of the MTFP.
findings.matters: Underspends that are planned rather than deficit-driven show improved budget management; peer councils assess whether this reflects changed demand or improved execution.
findings.figures: Underspend £4.066m; Children's Services underspend cited as first positive outturn in several years
findings.quote: The Council delivered a draft financial outturn for 2025/26 of an underspend of £4.066m... For the first time in several years Children's Services has underspent, this is testament to the successful delivery of prevention and early help services.

findings.headline: General reserves rebuilt to 4.6% of spend, within the 3-5% target band, after historic lows.
findings.detail: The council has replenished reserves through financial strategy and improved spending control. This reverses a period of reserve depletion that had forced the council into short-term borrowing for cash management. The position supports financial resilience and reduces reliance on external financing.
findings.matters: Reserve levels determine a council's headroom to absorb spending shocks; peer councils and lenders watch this metric closely as an indicator of financial stability.
findings.figures: General reserve balances at 4.6% of net general fund spend; target range 3-5%
findings.quote: General reserve balances have been replenished to 4.6% (recommended levels are between 3% and 5%)

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Derby Grouped Schools Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract Expiry
findings.headline: NISTA first PFI expiry health check expected in 2026; council establishing formal project governance with dedicated Senior Responsible Officer
findings.detail: The council expects NISTA to conduct the first of three recommended Expiry Health Checks in 2026, using a red/amber/green rating system to assess readiness. Red or red/amber actions trigger 6-month follow-up reviews. The Director of Commissioning and Delivery is appointed as Senior Responsible Officer, with a dedicated PFI Expiry Project Team established across Finance, Legal, Property, Estates, Procurement, Commissioning, and HR.
findings.matters: Independent government readiness assessments provide accountability and structured monitoring against standard criteria; RAG ratings will signal progress or slippage and potentially affect government support or lender confidence.
findings.figures: First health check 2026; three health checks over seven-year period; 6-month follow-up on red/amber actions
findings.quote: NISTA will produce a written report following the Expiry Health Check and will rate the project's readiness for expiry using a RAG (red/amber/green) rating system. Any actions listed as red or red/amber are followed up after 6 months.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Derby Grouped Schools Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract Expiry
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation may require PFI contract novation to successor authority if reorganisation proceeds before December 2031 expiry date
findings.detail: The council identifies that local government reorganisation timescales may align with PFI expiry, potentially requiring the contract to be novated from Derby City Council to a successor authority. The paper emphasises the need to establish clear governance, confirm accountability post-reorganisation, and ensure continuity of expertise and decision-making, including appointment of an empowered Senior Responsible Officer.
findings.matters: Creates uncertainty over contractual continuity and management accountability; reorganisation during the critical expiry period could disrupt delivery, create expertise gaps, and delay handover negotiations with academy trusts.
findings.figures: 31 December 2031 PFI expiry date; Local Government Reorganisation timescale uncertain
findings.quote: Due to the timing of the expiry of the PFI contract expiry and the timescales involved in the Local Government Reorganisation, there may be a requirement that the PFI contract is novated from Derby City Council to the new successor local authority

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Derby Grouped Schools Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract Expiry
findings.headline: Department for Education funding initial condition surveys of PFI schools in June 2026; further surveys planned at five, three and one year before expiry
findings.detail: The Department for Education is funding and conducting initial condition surveys on all PFI schools approaching expiry, with the Grouped Schools PFI schools' surveys scheduled for late June 2026. NISTA recommends surveys at five, three, and one year before contract expiry to identify defects with sufficient time for rectification. Any issues not addressed by the PFI contractor before expiry could leave academy trusts or council liable for post-contract maintenance.
findings.matters: Early identification of asset condition issues reduces risk of unexpected post-contract liabilities; DfE funding of initial surveys reduces first-year cost to council; demonstrates alignment with government-recommended seven-year planning horizon.
findings.figures: Initial surveys June 2026; follow-up surveys at five, three, and one year before 31 December 2031 expiry
findings.quote: The DfE is now funding and undertaking initial condition surveys on all PFI schools approaching expiry and will be carrying out surveys of the Grouped Schools PFI schools in late June 2026.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Derby Grouped Schools Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract Expiry
findings.headline: Responsibility for facilities management at five schools transfers to academy trusts at 2031 PFI expiry, not to council; council retains liability for transition
findings.detail: All five schools in the contract have converted to academy status since it was signed. At 31 December 2031 expiry, responsibility for buildings and facilities management services will pass to their Multi Academy Trusts, not to the council. Only Alvaston Children's Centre returns to the council. The council remains party to the PFI contract and must oversee the transition despite not controlling post-expiry operations, adding coordination complexity.
findings.matters: Council retains contractual liability but loses operational control, creating risk of disputes over asset condition, handover obligations, and allocation of post-contract costs between council and academy trusts.
findings.figures: 31 December 2031 expiry date; five schools to academy trusts; one centre to council
findings.quote: Although Derby City Council remains party to the Grouped Schools PFI contract on their behalf, responsibility for buildings and FM services will pass back to the relevant Multi Academy Trusts at the end of the contract in December 2031, adding an extra layer to the expiry process.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Derby Grouped Schools Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract Expiry
findings.headline: PFI exit reserve established with £1.316 million but £0.084 million shortfall identified for 2026/27, requiring Budget Risk Reserve funding
findings.detail: A PFI exit reserve was established at 2025/26 outturn with £1.316 million transferred from underspends. The 2026/27 requirement is approximately £1.4 million, creating an identified shortfall of £0.084 million. If not met from alternative resources, this will be funded from the Budget Risk Reserve, reducing general contingency available for other budget pressures.
findings.matters: First-year costs exceeded reserve estimate, requiring use of budget risk contingency; future years' increases must be managed through the MTFP, creating demand on council capacity.
findings.figures: PFI exit reserve £1.316m; 2026/27 requirement £1.4m; shortfall £0.084m
findings.quote: For 2026/27 this will include use of the Budget Risk Reserve for the shortfall identified of approximately £0.084m if other resource has not been identified.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Derby Grouped Schools Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract Expiry
findings.headline: PFI contract expiry programme estimated at £5 million over five years, with £1.4 million required in 2026/27 for legal, technical advisors and project staffing
findings.detail: The council has established a five-year expiry management programme with estimated costs of £5 million. In 2026/27 alone, £1.4 million is required: £1.275 million for legal and financial contracts and £0.125 million for staffing. The programme includes condition surveys, lifecycle reviews, specialist advisors, and stakeholder coordination structured as a formal project.
findings.matters: A material, fixed-timeline expenditure with budget implications across two MTFP cycles; lack of early resourcing commitment risks delays or unidentified post-contract liabilities for council or academy trusts.
findings.figures: £5 million estimated over five years; £1.4m required in 2026/27; £1.275m legal and financial; £0.125m staffing
findings.quote: There is a requirement to spend approximately £1.4m in 2026/27, which consists of financial and legal contracts associated with expiry totalling £1.275m and additional staffing costs of circa £0.125m.

findings.headline: Net debt £556.604m, reduced from £602.537m; council refinancing to medium/long-term PWLB to manage interest rate risk
findings.detail: Gross external debt stands at £666.286m offset by investments of £109.682m, resulting in net debt of £556.604m (improved from £602.537m prior year). Council is actively refinancing short-term loans into medium/long-term PWLB borrowing to mitigate interest rate risk. Cashflow managed through short-to-medium term borrowing to avoid locking in higher long-term rates. Treasury Management reserve receiving £4.973m transfer to support future capital borrowing.
findings.matters: Debt position and active refinancing strategy indicate approach to interest rate risk management. Reserve-building acknowledges that high-rate environment is creating cost pressures requiring ongoing close management.
findings.figures: Gross debt £666.286m; investments £109.682m; net debt £556.604m (prior £602.537m); TM reserve transfer £4.973m
findings.quote: As at the 31 March 2026, the total debt portfolio of the Council (including HRA debt) is £666.286m offset by investments of (£109.682m) resulting in an overall net debt position of £556.604m.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit £2.291m (council's share £1.633m); council tax collection 92.52%, business rates 96.46%
findings.detail: Collection Fund outturn is a deficit of £2.291m, with the council's share of £1.633m classified as a one-off pressure to be managed through medium-term planning and smoothing reserves. Council tax collected £151.610m of £163.858m billed (92.52%) and business rates collected £99.833m of £103.5m billed (96.46%). These collection rates are reasonable but the deficit reflects post-pandemic recovery timing.
findings.matters: Collection rates directly impact cash flow and revenue sustainability. The deficit indicates timing mismatches between billing and collection requiring reserve smoothing and creating a headwind into 2026/27.
findings.figures: Collection Fund deficit £2.291m; council's share £1.633m; Council tax collection 92.52%; Business rates 96.46%
findings.quote: The actual overall Collection Fund deficit is £2.291m with the Council's share of this being £1.633m. This one-off pressure will be reflected in the medium-term planning of the council as appropriate and there will be use of the smoothing reserves as required.

findings.headline: Children's social care underspend reported for first time in several years; looked after children caseload down to 512 from 551
findings.detail: Children's social care underspent for first time in several years, with looked after children numbers declining from 551 to 512 (reduction of 39). Budget scrutinised weekly on value-for-money. While higher-cost agency placements increased slightly, lower-cost placement types decreased more significantly, demonstrating improved placement mix and early intervention effectiveness.
findings.matters: Children's social care has historically been a pressure area watched by lenders. A turnaround in trend, even if modest, signals improved demand management and early intervention success.
findings.figures: Looked after children: 512 at 31 March 2026 vs 551 at Q3; reduction 39 children
findings.quote: It is pleasing to report that for the first time in a number of years children's social care has underspent.

findings.headline: Strategic Housing initiatives reduce temporary B&B accommodation by £0.620m; families in emergency housing down from 248 to 211
findings.detail: Temporary bed and breakfast spending fell by £0.620m through Abbey Lodge (supported accommodation) and reformed singles intervention. Families in B&B accommodation reduced from 248 to 211 (year-on-year), and Housing Benefit recovery improved from 80% to 88%, indicating both reduced reliance on expensive emergency housing and improved cost recovery.
findings.matters: Homelessness and temporary accommodation is a major pressure area for councils nationally and closely monitored by lenders. This demonstrates active management reversing the trend and reducing exposure to volatile spending.
findings.figures: B&B underspend £0.620m; families in B&B: 211 vs 248 prior year; Housing Benefit recovery 88% vs 80%
findings.quote: These initiatives have both mitigated against the number of B&B nights required by service users (211 compared with 248 families in accommodation this time last year) and increased Housing Benefit recovery (up to 88% from 80% recovery), improving the financial position above that reported at Q3.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account surplus £4.424m, £3.055m better than budgeted £1.369m
findings.detail: HRA delivered a surplus of £4.424m against a budgeted surplus of £1.369m, positive variance of £3.055m (223% of forecast). Improvement attributed to higher than budgeted rental and service charge income, lower than anticipated increase in bad debt provision, and lower than expected capital charges. This outperformance provides headroom for housing investment.
findings.matters: HRA financial strength directly underpins housing investment capacity and debt servicing capability. Performance materially better than forecast indicates strong rent collection, tenant arrears management, and cost control.
findings.figures: Surplus £4.424m vs budget £1.369m; variance £3.055m
findings.quote: The HRA shows a positive variance of (£3.055m) this year, with a surplus of (£4.424m) against the budgeted surplus of (£1.369m).

findings.headline: All planned savings of £9.861m delivered at 100% across all directorates in 2025/26
findings.detail: Savings targets totalling £9.861m were fully achieved: Peoples Services £5.955m, Communities and Place £1.456m, Chief Executives £2.450m. Complete delivery across all service areas without slippage validates budget planning assumptions and demonstrates management capability to deliver difficult decisions.
findings.matters: Full achievement of planned savings demonstrates credibility of the budgeting process and management's operational capability to execute reductions. This provides confidence in forward-looking MTFP and signals capacity to manage future pressures.
findings.figures: Total savings target £9.861m; delivery 100%
findings.quote: 100% of the Councils savings target of £9.861m for 2025/26 has been achieved.

findings.headline: General Fund delivered £4.066m underspend, transferred entirely to reserves rather than drawing down Budget Risk Reserve
findings.detail: Council reported a £4.066m general fund underspend, transferred wholly to reserves to establish contingency for future pressures. The report emphasises this demonstrates "financial resilience" despite "several years" of challenging position with reduced national funding, pandemic impacts, and global fiscal instability. This reserve-building contrasts with the prior pattern of reserve depletion described in the report's context.
findings.matters: Reserve-building in-year signals underlying financial management capability rather than reliance on one-off solutions. Not drawing down the Budget Risk Reserve indicates structural control and reduced dependency on contingency funds.
findings.figures: £4.066m underspend transferred to reserves
findings.quote: By successfully maintaining its financial resilience the Council has not drawn down the Budget Risk reserve to balance the budget and instead, accomplished a contribution to reserves to meet future financial uncertainties.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reaches £23.274m; government commits approximately 90% funding of historic High Needs deficit
findings.detail: Derby's DSG has accumulated a £23.274m cumulative deficit by end of 2025/26, with an in-year deficit of £7.085m driven by High Needs Block overspending. The paper identifies this as creating an estimated £2m annual treasury cost to the general fund. The government has committed to provide a High Needs Stability Grant covering approximately 90% of each authority's DSG deficit accrued to end of 2025/26 (worth approximately £21m for Derby), contingent on approval of the Local SEND Reform Plan, expected by late autumn 2026.
findings.matters: DSG deficits represent a contingent liability eroding general fund sustainability. While government support is committed, the condition (plan approval) and timing uncertainty create planning risk for the near term.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £23.274m; in-year deficit £7.085m; government grant approximately £21m (90% of deficit); estimated annual general fund treasury cost circa £2m
findings.quote: All local authorities with a SEND deficit will be eligible in 2026/27 to receive a High Needs Stability Grant covering approximately 90% of their High Needs related DSG deficit accrued up to the end of 2025/26.

findings.committee: Communities, Public Protection and Housing Scrutiny Review Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Housing Supply and Statutory Duties Presentation
findings.headline: Right to Buy sales have reduced housing stock by 376 dwellings over three years, averaging 125 per year but reducing
findings.detail: RTB sales averaged 125 per year but are reducing due to recent RTB policy changes. Over the last three years, 376 dwellings were lost through RTB sales. The paper notes these losses are impacting the council's ability to meet housing need and supply targets.
findings.matters: RTB sales reduce both the council's housing asset base and rental income, which affects HRA financial position and sustainability. For lenders, persistent RTB sales erode the asset base backing HRA finances.
findings.figures: 376 dwellings lost three years; 125 average per year (reducing)
findings.quote: Losses through RTB (376 dwellings in last 3 years) are also impacting [and] RTB sales Avg 125 per year but reducing due to recent RTB changes

findings.committee: Communities, Public Protection and Housing Scrutiny Review Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Housing Supply and Statutory Duties Presentation
findings.headline: HRA Delivery Programme targets 66 completions in 2025/26 and 139 homes in 2026/27, combining new build and acquisitions
findings.detail: The HRA plans 66 completions for 2025/26 (30 new build and 33 open market acquisitions). For 2026/27, the target is 139 homes (97 new build, 32 acquisitions, 10 direct purchases). The pipeline includes multiple sites in various delivery stages. The council is also developing a 90-unit extra care development at Bramblebrook.
findings.matters: The capital investment programme has funding and delivery implications for the HRA and council borrowing. For lenders, this shows commitment to address supply gap but signals ongoing capital requirements.
findings.figures: 66 completions 2025/26 (30 new build, 33 acquisitions); 139 target 2026/27 (97 new build, 32 acquisitions, 10 direct purchase); 90-unit extra care development
findings.quote: Forecasts for affordable housing delivery 2025/26 and 2026/27 – between 375 and 569 affordable dwellings in total over the two years

findings.committee: Communities, Public Protection and Housing Scrutiny Review Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Housing Supply and Statutory Duties Presentation
findings.headline: 701 households and 779 children in temporary accommodation, with council noting costs and impacts on wider services
findings.detail: As of 2024/25, 302 families and 399 singles/childless couples were placed into temporary accommodation. There are currently 779 children in temporary accommodation. The paper identifies this as creating 'Costs and impacts on Council and wider services'. The council is managing this through acquiring Lonsdale Place (49-95 flats) and remodelling Ashover Lodge.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a substantial ongoing cost pressure on council budgets. For lenders, elevated temporary accommodation placements signal financial stress and demand-led service pressures.
findings.figures: 302 families; 399 singles/couples; 701 total households; 779 children; 49 expanding to 95 flats
findings.quote: Families placed into temporary accommodation 24/25 302 [and] Children currently in temporary accommodation 779 [and] Costs and impacts on Council and wider services

findings.committee: Communities, Public Protection and Housing Scrutiny Review Board
findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Housing Supply and Statutory Duties Presentation
findings.headline: Council faces gap of 486 homes per year between identified need of 672 and average delivery of 190
findings.detail: Over 2020/21 to 2024/25, the council delivered 951 affordable homes (averaging 190 per year), against Local Housing Needs Assessment evidence of need for 672 per year (3,360 over five years). This creates a gap of 486 homes per year (2,430 over five years). The council forecasts delivering between 375 and 569 homes over 2025/26 and 2026/27.
findings.matters: Large unmet housing demand translates directly to temporary accommodation placements, which are a significant cost pressure on council budgets and wider services.
findings.figures: 672 per year need; 190 per year average delivery; 486 per year gap; 2,430 five-year gap; 375-569 forecast 2025/26-26/27
findings.quote: LHNA evidenced need 672 per year (3,360 over last 5 years) [and] Gap between identified need and delivery 486 homes per year (2,430 over last 5 years)

findings.committee: Communities, Public Protection and Housing Scrutiny Review Board
findings.paper_title: Late Item - Housing Supply and Statutory Duties
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account Business Plan approval required by January 2026 to support stock investment and new affordable housing
findings.detail: Within the 2025–26 Business Plan, the council planned to formulate, consult on and secure approval of a balanced HRA Business Plan by January 2026 to support investment in council housing stock and new affordable housing. The paper notes the HRA Business Plan is reviewed annually. This document is dated April 2026; approval status is not reported.
findings.matters: HRA decisions drive capital spending and housing investment decisions affecting the council's balance sheet; the stated aim to balance the HRA while investing signals the council is seeking to manage housing supply pressures without running an HRA deficit
findings.figures: January 2026 approval deadline (now past)
findings.quote: Formulating, consulting on and securing approval of a balanced Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Business Plan by January 2026, supporting investment in our stock and new affordable housing. The BP is reviewed annually.

findings.committee: Communities, Public Protection and Housing Scrutiny Review Board
findings.paper_title: Late Item - Housing Supply and Statutory Duties
findings.headline: Risk of non-compliant use of bed and breakfast placements and inability to fully meet accommodation sufficiency duties for homelessness and social care
findings.detail: Due to lack of housing and reduced social housing turnover, the council faces risk of non-compliant use of B&B placements and inability to fully meet accommodation sufficiency duties for homelessness, Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care, domestic abuse victims and specialist complex needs accommodation.
findings.matters: Statutory non-compliance is a regulatory and reputational risk; B&B usage is costly; the risk indicates housing pressures are creating service delivery failures across multiple council functions
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Risk of non-compliant use of B&B placements and inability to fully meet accommodation sufficiency duties for homelessness, Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care, domestic abuse victims and specialist complex needs accommodation.

findings.committee: Communities, Public Protection and Housing Scrutiny Review Board
findings.paper_title: Late Item - Housing Supply and Statutory Duties
findings.headline: Housing and accommodation sufficiency identified as cross-cutting risk with consequences including non-compliance with statutory duties and increased costs across systems
findings.detail: The council's Strategic and Place risk registers identify housing supply and accommodation sufficiency as impacting homelessness, Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care, domestic abuse, refugees and asylum seekers, and complex needs. The paper states the consequences are non-compliance with statutory duties and increased costs across systems, with knock-on cost pressures for health, education and other public services.
findings.matters: Increased costs across multiple council services due to housing pressures represent expenditure that will affect the council's financial position; risk of statutory non-compliance creates regulatory and reputational risk
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Strategic and Place risk registers identify housing supply and accommodation sufficiency as cross-cutting risks impacting homelessness, Adult Social Care, Children's Social Care, domestic abuse, refugees and asylum seekers, and those with complex needs. Consequences include non-compliance with statutory duties and increased costs across systems.

findings.headline: Council adopts short-term borrowing strategy, deferring long-term debt in anticipation of lower interest rates
findings.detail: With short-term rates falling and expected to decline further, Derby is using internal resources and short- to medium-term borrowing rather than locking in current long-term rates, betting on more favorable long-term borrowing conditions becoming available.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of when the council will refinance or require new long-term debt; peer councils are watching how others manage rate-timing decisions in the current environment.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: It is likely more cost-effective to use internal resources or short- to medium-term borrowing until favorable long-term borrowing options arise

findings.headline: Money Market Fund investment limits increased from £7m to £10m for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council is raising the maximum it can hold in short-term money market funds from £7m to £10m from 2026/27, suggesting either increased liquid cash available or an adjusted approach to cash management.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's cash position and available liquidity; peer finance directors want to see how other councils adapt treasury parameters to current conditions.
findings.figures: £7m to £10m
findings.quote: Money Market Fund Limits have been increased from £7m to £10m from 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: Elector correspondence received from two sources, including over 130 emails, though neither accepted as formal valid objection
findings.detail: Auditors received correspondence from two sources during the audit period. One related to a contractual dispute over an immaterial sum; the other involved over 130 emails. Neither met the threshold for a formal objection to the accounts requiring audit investigation. The volume of emails (130+) from the second correspondent suggests significant concern or dissatisfaction from that party.
findings.matters: Whilst neither objection was formally valid, the number of emails (130+) indicates a substantive complaint from one party. Multiple external complaints may signal underlying service issues or stakeholder dissatisfaction even if not material to the audit.
findings.figures: Two sources of correspondence; one involved over 130 emails
findings.quote: We received correspondence from two sources: one correspondence related to a contractual dispute between the council for an immaterial sum; the other involved over 130 emails; but neither were accepted as valid objections.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: Audit fees reduced to £223k from £316k prior year due to curtailed substantive testing on financial statements
findings.detail: Audit fees fell by 29% year-on-year, primarily because substantive testing on the statement of accounts was not completed due to backstop constraints. Work on statement of accounts reduced from £124k to £77k. Value for Money work fees remained flat at £139k. Fee reduction reflects reduced audit scope and lower assurance, not efficiency gains.
findings.matters: Lower fees should not be interpreted as improved audit efficiency; they reflect the auditor's inability to complete testing due to the backstop deadline, meaning less audit work was performed and less assurance provided to users.
findings.figures: 2024/25 total fees: £223,091 vs 2023/24: £316,028. Statement of accounts work: £77,441 vs £124,494 prior year. VFM fees: £138,650 both years
findings.quote: Work completed: statement of accounts (including review of areas deemed significant (Section 03)) £77,441

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: Year-end bank reconciliation timing corrected: council now reconciles as at 31 March instead of 28 March
findings.detail: Prior audit identified that the council was performing year-end bank reconciliation on 28 March (last working day of the month) rather than 31 March, making external verification difficult. Recommendation was made to reconcile on the final day of the year. Council has now implemented this and performed reconciliation as at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: Bank reconciliation is a fundamental control. Correction demonstrates council is responding to audit recommendations and remedying control deficiencies, and improves auditability of cash positions.
findings.figures: Prior year reconciliation date: 28 March 2024. Current year: 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Council performed its year end bank reconciliation as at 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: Data migration control deficiencies remain unresolved after multiple audit years; no documented cleansing strategy or management sign-off on approach
findings.detail: Two IT control deficiencies identified in prior audits relating to TechnologyOne system migration remain outstanding. Auditors found no evidence of pre-migration data cleanse strategy and no documented management approval of the migration approach. Current update states "No additional update in the current year" though management notes internal audit reviewed the project. The absence of formal procedures creates risk of incomplete or inaccurate data migration and loss of transaction records.
findings.matters: System data integrity is foundational to financial reporting. Multi-year unresolved data migration deficiencies suggest either slow remediation or inadequate control documentation that could mask underlying data quality issues.
findings.figures: Deficiency identified in prior audits; no resolution in current year or prior year
findings.quote: No additional update in the current year. Management noted that internal audit reviewed data migration as part of the project and that data migration was built into the overall implementation plan.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: Audit assurance rebuild timeline remains uncertain; no end date provided for the disclaimer period
findings.detail: Auditors state they will "continue to work closely with you and management to take the necessary steps to rebuild assurance over future accounting periods" but provide no target year for completion. The NAO guidance (LARRIG 06) acknowledges timescale "will vary between audit engagements and according to each audit's particular circumstances". A detailed rebuilding plan is promised as part of the 2025/26 Audit Strategy Memorandum.
findings.matters: Lenders need clarity on when audited accounts will be restored. An open-ended rebuild period creates ongoing uncertainty about the council's ability to obtain audit opinion and raises questions about the root causes if already five years have not sufficed.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years of disclaimers (2020/21 to 2024/25); rebuild timeline: to be provided in 2025/26 audit strategy
findings.quote: We will continue to work closely with you and management to take the necessary steps to rebuild assurance over future accounting periods.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: Value for Money arrangements found to be adequate; no significant weaknesses identified in financial sustainability, governance, or service efficiency
findings.detail: The auditor completed Value for Money work under the 2024 Code of Audit Practice and found no significant weaknesses in arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in the council's use of resources. Work covered three criteria: financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. No recommendations were required.
findings.matters: Positive finding demonstrates council has adequate arrangements for resource planning, financial management, and governance despite the audit qualification. Shows management processes for financial sustainability are in place even though the accounts themselves are unaudited.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: We have completed our work in respect of the Council's arrangements for the year ended 31 March 2025 and we have not identified any significant weaknesses in arrangements that have required us to make a recommendation.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: No substantive testing performed on account balances or transactions; financial statements remain untested for material misstatement
findings.detail: Due to backstop arrangements, auditors did not undertake substantive testing procedures on any balances or transactions in the accounts. No misstatements were identified because testing was not conducted, not because the accounts are error-free. This means the financial position presented has not been verified for accuracy.
findings.matters: Unaudited and untested accounts cannot provide lenders with assurance over asset valuations, debt levels, cash positions, or reserve levels. Lenders cannot rely on the reported financial position.
findings.figures: None: absence of testing means no audit work performed on account balances
findings.quote: Due to the backstop, we have not undertaken substantive testing procedures on any balances or transactions reported in the accounts. Consequently, there are no misstatements to report.

findings.paper_title: Item 4 - Appendix 1 - Report of the External Auditor
findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion issued for fifth consecutive financial year; opening balances remain unverified
findings.detail: Derby has received disclaimed audit opinions for 2020/21 through 2024/25 (five consecutive years). The current disclaimer is issued because auditors cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence on opening balances by the backstop date of 27 February 2026, a deadline set by the Accounts and Audit (Amendment) Regulations 2024. The National Audit Office guidance (LARRIG 06) issued in June 2025 acknowledges that rebuilding assurance timescale "will vary between audit engagements" but auditors have determined insufficient time remains before the mandatory publication deadline.
findings.matters: A council unable to produce an audited opinion for five consecutive years presents elevated credit risk to lenders. Unverified opening balances compound the audit limitation and create fundamental uncertainty about the accuracy of the reported financial position.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 27 February 2026. Disclaimer period: financial years 2020/21 to 2024/25
findings.quote: we are not able obtain sufficient appropriate evidence upon which to form an opinion on the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 before the 2026 backstop date

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Cover Report Audited Financial Statements 2024-25
findings.headline: Derby Council received a disclaimed audit opinion on 2024-25 accounts, continuing a pattern of limited audits, with auditors unable to adequately test all transactions.
findings.detail: Due to national audit backlogs and following previous disclaimed opinions, Forvis Mazars undertook only a limited audit of 2024-25. A disclaimed opinion allows auditors to complete their work where they cannot adequately test all transactions. The paper states that until underlying issues are resolved, a clean audit opinion is unlikely in the medium term.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions mean lenders and stakeholders cannot be confident in the completeness and accuracy of the council's financial statements; repeated limitations signal potential governance and financial control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: As a result of the previous disclaimed opinions, Forvis Mazars have again only been able to undertake a limited audit of the 2024/25 accounts, and this has inevitably led to a further 'disclaimed' opinion for 2024/25.

findings.committee: Urgent Leader of the Council Cabinet Member Meeting
findings.paper_title: Item 5 - SEND and Alternative Provision Capital Programme
findings.headline: Contract signature deadline of 20 February 2026 required to enable school opening in September 2026 and 60-place SEND capacity increase
findings.detail: Formal budget increase must be approved before works can be commissioned. Contractor must enter contract by 20 February 2026 to complete remaining phases and meet September 2026 opening target. Delay beyond this date would prevent opening and leave allocated SEND places unfilled. Council has confirmed placements; failure to deliver would trigger tribunal appeals from families with automatic right to redress.
findings.matters: Tight capital delivery timelines create cascading cost risks through project failure, ongoing high-cost out-of-authority placements versus in-borough provision, and potential tribunal costs from families with allocated places
findings.figures: Contract deadline 20 February 2026, opening date September 2026, provision of up to 100 students representing 60-place increase from current Castle School Newtons Walk capacity; in-borough cost £0.028m per pupil annually versus out-of-authority cost £0.080-0.120m per pupil annually
findings.quote: If the Council does not enter into the contract for works by 20 February 2026 it will not be possible to complete the works necessary to meet the planning conditions and to allow the school to open in September 2026.

findings.committee: Urgent Leader of the Council Cabinet Member Meeting
findings.paper_title: Item 5 - SEND and Alternative Provision Capital Programme
findings.headline: Approved budget for Castle School works increased from £0.8m to £2.553m due to unforeseen fire regulations, ventilation, and window insulation requirements
findings.detail: Purchase of St James House approved November 2024 with £0.8m works budget. Following property acquisition and detailed feasibility and design work, additional building regulation requirements identified beyond original scope, including fire safety upgrades, ventilation system replacement, and window replacement for noise insulation to meet planning conditions. Phase 1 works to third floor completed within approved budget; phase 2 completion now costs £2.553m total.
findings.matters: Peer authority finance directors managing SEND estate expansion need to understand capital project scoping risks; demonstrates that detailed feasibility conducted post-acquisition can reveal significant cost escalations requiring budget increase
findings.figures: £0.8m original approved budget, £2.553m new total budget, £1.753m increase required
findings.quote: the total cost of completing the works (delivering the remaining phases) has increased to £2.553m, requiring additional budget approval of £1.753m.

news_drafts.headline: Strategic housing alternatives to bed and breakfast accommodation delivering £0.463m underspend through direct matches and private sector leasing scheme
news_drafts.lead: Demonstrates that demand-side interventions creating alternatives to expensive temporary accommodation can reduce costs while maintaining service availability.

news_drafts.headline: Insurance costs reduced by £0.410m following contract renegotiation, delivering unexpected saving not forecast at budget setting
news_drafts.lead: Demonstrates the value of active commercial management; budget setting based on historical trends can miss genuine cost reduction opportunities.

news_drafts.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £58.9m to £933.704m; council pursuing short-term borrowing strategy at 4-4.5% due to elevated PWLB rates of 5-6.5%
news_drafts.lead: The rising CFR and short-term borrowing strategy expose the council to refinancing risk if rates do not fall, and create dependence on functioning debt markets.
